title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
description:
# Min Cost to Connect All Points

You are given `points`, where `points[i] = [xi, yi]` is the coordinate of the `i`th point on a 2D plane.

You may connect any two distinct points. The cost of connecting `points[i]` and `points[j]` is their Manhattan distance: `|xi - xj| + |yi - yj|`.

The selected connections must provide exactly one path between any two points. Their total cost is the sum of the selected connection costs. A single point needs no connection and costs `0`.

Return the lowest total cost satisfying these rules.

## Example 1

**Input:** `points = [[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]]`

**Output:** `20`

**Explanation:** One optimal tree connects `(0,0)-(2,2)`, `(2,2)-(5,2)`, `(5,2)-(7,0)`, and `(2,2)-(3,10)`, with total cost `4 + 3 + 4 + 9 = 20`.

## Example 2

**Input:** `points = [[3,12],[-2,5],[-4,1]]`

**Output:** `18`

## Constraints

- `1 <= points.length <= 1000`
- `-10^6 <= xi, yi <= 10^6`
- All pairs `(xi, yi)` are distinct.

solutions.name: Dense Prim with Distance Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Grow one connected component. For each point outside the component, store the cheapest edge that can connect it to any point already chosen. Repeatedly add the unchosen point with the smallest stored distance, then update all remaining distances using the newly added point.

## Key Insight

The graph is complete, so building every edge is expensive and unnecessary. Prim's cut property lets us keep only each outside point's best known crossing edge; scanning all points is fast enough for `n <= 1000` and uses only linear extra space.

## Complexity Analysis

There are `n` rounds and each round scans all points to choose the next vertex and all points again to update distances, so the time complexity is O(n^2). The `visited` and `minDist` arrays use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Kruskal with Union-Find
solutions.description:
## Approach

Generate every pairwise Manhattan edge, sort all edges by weight, and use Union-Find to accept an edge only when it connects two different components. Stop after accepting `n - 1` edges.

## Key Insight

Kruskal's algorithm is a direct greedy view of MST construction: take the cheapest edge that does not create a cycle. It is easy to reason about, but the complete graph has O(n^2) edges, so this route spends much more memory than dense Prim.

## Complexity Analysis

The algorithm creates and sorts O(n^2) edges, so the time complexity is O(n^2 log n). The edge list dominates the space complexity at O(n^2), while Union-Find uses O(n).

solutions.name: Lazy Prim with Priority Queue
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use Prim's algorithm with a min-heap of candidate edges. Whenever a point enters the tree, push edges from that point to every unvisited point. Pop the cheapest edge until it reaches a new point, add its cost, and continue.

## Key Insight

This version mirrors the usual heap-based Prim template and is useful when the graph is sparse. In this problem the graph is complete, so the heap may hold many stale candidate edges; it is simpler to adapt but not as memory efficient as the distance-array version.

## Complexity Analysis

Each accepted point can push O(n) candidate edges, giving O(n^2) heap entries and O(n^2 log n) time. The heap can grow to O(n^2) space in the worst case.

solutions.name: Boruvka Component Merging
solutions.description:
## Approach

Start with every point as its own component. In each phase, scan all point pairs and remember the cheapest outgoing edge for every current component. Add all chosen safe edges with Union-Find, reducing the number of components until only one remains.

## Key Insight

Boruvka's algorithm gives a third classic MST perspective: each component independently takes its cheapest edge across the cut, and all of those choices are safe. It reinforces why greedy MST edges can be added in batches, not only one at a time.

## Complexity Analysis

Each phase scans O(n^2) pairs, and the number of components at least halves after successful phases in the standard Boruvka analysis, so the time complexity is O(n^2 log n). Union-Find plus the cheapest-edge arrays use O(n) extra space.

tests.description: Canonical five-point set whose minimum spanning tree has total Manhattan cost twenty.
Negative coordinates verify Manhattan distance across quadrants.
A single point needs no connecting edge.
Two points require exactly one edge.
Collinear points should connect through adjacent gaps instead of a long direct edge.
A square has many optimal MSTs with equal edge weights.
A center-ish point changes the cheapest tree but does not connect every corner directly.
Symmetric negative and positive coordinates create tied MST choices.
Large coordinate extremes stay within 32-bit total cost for this constraint range.
All pairwise distances tie, so solutions must handle arbitrary valid MST structure.
